stimulus.text: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796: “It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.” Washington also warned, in the most solemn manner, against “the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally,” saying it “serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration.” The address was published in a Philadelphia newspaper, not delivered as a speech, as Washington left office after two terms.
stimulus.source_note: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quotes George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796, public domain.
stem: Why is Washington’s Farewell Address also remembered as a precedent of the presidency?

options.text: It was the first time a president spoke to Congress in person.
options.misconception: The address was published in a newspaper, not delivered as a speech.

options.text: It announced he would not seek a third term, setting the two-term example.
It created the president’s cabinet of department heads.
options.misconception: Background: Washington had set up the cabinet at the start of his presidency, not in 1796.

options.text: It gave the president the power to make treaties alone.
options.misconception: Background: treaties still needed the Senate’s consent; the address did not change that.

rationales.B: Background: Washington left office after two terms, and no president served more than two until Franklin Roosevelt in the 1940s.
rationales.A: The address was published in a newspaper, not delivered as a speech.
rationales.C: The cabinet was set up earlier in his presidency, not in this address.
rationales.D: The address did not change how treaties are made.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus says the address was published as Washington left office after two terms.
2. Background: by leaving after two terms, Washington set an example every president followed until Franklin Roosevelt in the 1940s.
3. The address was his farewell because he was choosing not to run again.
4. So it is remembered as a precedent for the two-term presidency, not for speeches, cabinets, or treaties.
Remember: a farewell is a precedent when the leaving itself becomes the rule others follow.
